body.message: A standard discounted cash flow valuation isn't suitable for Rivian Automotive, Inc. No intrinsic value is reported, deliberately: the model would produce a figure with no economic meaning.
reasons:
The company is loss-making: its day-to-day business lost $3.6bn in its 2025 financial year, and it made a loss in 4 of the last 4 years.
    This kind of valuation assumes a business that already makes a profit and grows steadily. Applying it to a loss-making company would mean inventing the profits it then puts a value on.

assumptions.name: revenue_growth
assumptions.detail: 3-year revenue CAGR, FY2022-FY2025 (1.7bn -> 5.4bn); raw 48.1% clamped to [0%, 15%]

assumptions.name: operating_margin
assumptions.detail: median operatingIncome / revenue over 3 years

assumptions.name: tax_rate
assumptions.detail: no profitable year in window; used US statutory rate

assumptions.name: da_pct
assumptions.detail: median D&A / revenue over 3 years

assumptions.name: capex_pct
assumptions.detail: median capex / revenue over 3 years

assumptions.name: nwc_pct
assumptions.detail: aggregate change in NWC / change in revenue, FY2022-FY2025

assumptions.name: wacc
assumptions.detail: CAPM: 5.00% + 1.67x5.50% = 14.16% equity; debt 6.56% (5.19% after tax); weights 78.8%E / 21.2%D

assumptions.name: terminal_growth
assumptions.detail: global default (~long-run nominal GDP growth)

assumptions.name: projection_years
assumptions.detail: modelling convention

body.disclaimer: Rivian Automotive, Inc. loses money, so a standard valuation was refused: it has no profits to project. This figure is not a valuation and must not be treated as one. It was produced only because it was explicitly requested, and it rests entirely on assumptions about a future that has not happened: that revenue grows 8.4% a year, that the operating margin climbs from -67% to 10% within 6 years, that the company can fund about $9.9bn of losses along the way, and that it then performs like an established, profitable business indefinitely. Loss-making companies often never reach sustained profitability; many raise money on terms that dilute existing shareholders, and some fail outright, in which case shareholders can lose everything. Modest changes to these assumptions move this figure by multiples, not percentages - the sensitivity table shows how far. It is not investment advice, a price target, or a reason to buy or sell.

The company is loss-making: its day-to-day business lost $3.6bn in its 2025 financial year, and it made a loss in 4 of the last 4 years.
    This kind of valuation assumes a business that already makes a profit and grows steadily. Applying it to a loss-making company would mean inventing the profits it then puts a value on.

assumptions.name: speculative_revenue_growth
assumptions.detail: the lower of the latest year's revenue growth (8.4%) and the 3-year CAGR (48.1%), so an early ramp from a small base is not extrapolated

assumptions.name: target_operating_margin
assumptions.detail: a generic mature-company operating margin. It is not specific to this company or its industry, and the company has never earned it

assumptions.name: years_to_profitability
assumptions.detail: the distance from today's -67% operating margin to the 10% target, closed at 15 percentage points a year - a fast pace to sustain

assumptions.name: post_profitability_growth
assumptions.detail: half the 8.4% assumed until profitability, as growth slows with scale; floored at terminal growth

assumptions.name: mature_capex_pct
assumptions.detail: 5% of revenue, typical of a mature business - today's build-out rate of 23.1% is not assumed to last. Depreciation is assumed to equal capex once mature

assumptions.name: mature_nwc_pct
assumptions.detail: the company's working-capital investment of 28.7% of revenue growth, limited to [0%, 10%] once mature

assumptions.name: tax_rate
assumptions.detail: US statutory rate. A loss-maker's tax history says nothing about a profitable future, and accumulated tax losses that would shelter early profits are not credited, which errs low

assumptions.name: wacc
assumptions.detail: CAPM: 5.00% + 1.67x5.50% = 14.16% equity; debt 6.56% (5.19% after tax); weights 78.8%E / 21.2%D

assumptions.name: terminal_growth
assumptions.detail: global default (~long-run nominal GDP growth), shared with the DCF

assumptions.name: projection_years
assumptions.detail: years of mature-company forecast after profitability, before the terminal value

wacc_inputs.name: beta
wacc_inputs.detail: computed from 57 monthly returns vs ^GSPC (5y), matching Yahoo's convention

wacc_inputs.name: cost_of_debt
wacc_inputs.detail: median interest expense / average debt (FY2025, FY2024, FY2023, FY2022)

warnings: On this path Rivian Automotive, Inc. burns $9.9bn of cash before turning profitable, against $6.1bn of cash and investments today. It would have to raise the difference, most likely by issuing shares that dilute existing holders - if it can raise it at all. The estimate subtracts the cost of those losses but assumes the money is found.

Rivian Automotive, Inc.'s gross margin was 3% in its 2025 financial year, below the 10% operating margin assumed. Reaching it needs gross margin to rise well above today's level before operating costs are even covered.
Even on these assumptions, the losses on the way and the debt outweigh the value of the profitable business at the end, so the estimate is negative.

Rivian Automotive, Inc. currently ties up an unusually large amount of cash in stock and unpaid customer bills as it grows. The estimate assumes this settles to a more typical level once the business matures.

body.message: A standard discounted cash flow valuation isn't suitable for American Express Company. No intrinsic value is reported, deliberately: the model would produce a figure with no economic meaning.
reasons: American Express Company is a Credit Services company whose interest expense is 11% of its revenue. Borrowing is part of how it earns that revenue rather than how it is financed, so - as for a bank - unlevered free cash flow and an enterprise-to-equity bridge are not meaningful, and a DCF would produce a figure with no economic meaning. A dividend discount model is not substituted either: it counts only dividends, and American Express Company returned $5.8bn through buybacks against $2.3bn in dividends in its 2025 financial year, so it would understate what shareholders receive. The appropriate tool is an excess-return model, which values a lender from its return on equity against its cost of equity. That model is not available yet, so no value is reported.

body.message: No speculative estimate is produced for QuantumScape Corporation. It was refused a standard valuation because it loses money, and even a projected path to profitability does not apply to it. No figure is reported, deliberately.
reasons: The company reported no revenue in its 2025 financial year. The valuation projects future revenue, so without any to start from there is nothing to project.

The company is loss-making: its day-to-day business lost $473m in its 2025 financial year, and it made a loss in 4 of the last 4 years.
    This kind of valuation assumes a business that already makes a profit and grows steadily. Applying it to a loss-making company would mean inventing the profits it then puts a value on.

QuantumScape Corporation reported no revenue in its 2025 financial year. A path to profitability grows revenue until it covers costs; with no revenue, both the revenue and the margins would have to be invented, which makes any figure fiction rather than speculation.
